author: Damonzwicker
raw_text:
Following up on the claimType thread from the ERC-8004 / ERC-8274 discussion — here is the worked example I committed to, covering field mapping,  recordPointer , and the  commitmentProof  /  outcomeEvidence  distinction. 
 claimType belongs in the signed artifact 
 The architectural reason is the one the thread has been circling around:  proofSystem  belongs to the verifier path and has contract context;  claimType  belongs inside the signed artifact and travels without that context. 
 An off-chain consumer holding only the raw struct should not need a registry lookup just to understand the accountability model of the claim. 
 These fields are therefore not redundant: 
 
 proofSystem  answers: what cryptographic mechanism authenticated the artifact? 
 claimType  answers: what kind of accountability model backs the claim? 
 
 For example, a zkVM proof system could back a deterministic re-execution claim, but a proof system alone does not tell a consumer whether the artifact should be treated as re-execution, attestation, or judgment. 
 Proposed enum: 
 enum ClaimType {
    ReExecution,  // deterministic computation — objectively disputable
    Attestation,  // authorized signer certifies a result
    Judgment      // subjective assessment — accountable through track record / policy
}
 
 verify() semantics for judgment claims 
 This is the category boundary the spec should protect explicitly. 
 For  ClaimType.Judgment ,  verify() = true  means the verdict is authentically the validator’s and correctly bound to the task inputs. It does not mean the judgment is sound, that the action should proceed, or that the verdict has been independently endorsed. 
 A settlement contract that gates directly on the bool has confirmed authenticity. It has not endorsed the judgment. 
 The three-layer boundary: 
 IProofVerifier  — authenticates the verdict
IAgentVerifier  — checks authorization for the task
recordPointer   — carries accountability: track record + pre-outcome commitment
 
 Verdict weight lives in the accountability record, not in the bool. 
 recordPointer schema 
 recordPointer  is load-bearing for judgment validators and optional for other claim types. 
 struct RecordPointer {
    bytes32 validatorId;
    bytes32 registryType;  // EVM registry, Nostr profile, off-chain ledger, etc.
    bytes   registryRef;   // registry-specific locator
    bytes   commitmentProof;
    bytes   outcomeEvidence;  // MAY be empty at verification time
}
 
 These answer different questions at different times in a dispute: 
 
 commitmentProof  answers: was this verdict committed before the outcome was known? 
 outcomeEvidence  answers: was the verdict later right or wrong? 
 
 commitmentProof  can be checked immediately, while  outcomeEvidence  may not exist until the outcome settles. 
 For the Nostr relay pattern  @babyblueviper1  described, the verifier would fetch the event by id from the declared relay set, verify the event id and signature, and then evaluate the publication evidence under that profile’s trust model. That maps architecturally onto ERC-8281’s commitment discipline: sign or commit first, publish to an independently retrievable location, then verify inclusion later. 
 The alignment is architectural rather than requiring one storage backend. The anchor may be a Nostr event, an on-chain OCP / ERC-8281 commitment, or another independently verifiable inclusion record. 
 Collapsing  commitmentProof  and  outcomeEvidence  into a single generic evidence field loses the ability to verify commitment integrity while the outcome is still open. For judgment validators, that distinction is the accountability model. 
 Field mapping summary 
 
 
 
 
 claimType 
 proofSystem examples 
 Accountability 
 Dispute surface 
 
 
 
 
 ReExecution 
 zk/sp1 ,  zk/ezkl ,  op/ora 
 Mathematical / economic 
 Objectively disputable 
 
 
 Attestation 
 sig/eip712 ,  attestation/wyriwe ,  attestation/multisig 
 Signer authorization / stake / reputation 
 Signer registry or policy 
 
 
 Judgment 
 sig/eip712 ,  attestation/judgment 
 Track record / reputation / policy-defined stake 
 Pre-outcome commitment + later outcome evidence 
 
 
 
 The important point is that  proofSystem  and  claimType  answer different questions. The former identifies the authentication mechanism. The latter identifies the assurance and accountability model. 
 Happy to shape the  recordPointer  schema further against  @babyblueviper1 ’s production struct and the v0.2 interfaces if that helps land the judgment variant as specified rather than implied. 
 — Damon ( @damonzwicker )

author: babyblueviper1
raw_text:
@Damonzwicker  the field-mapping table is the cleanest statement of the layering anywhere in these threads — three accountability models, three dispute surfaces, and  proofSystem  orthogonal to all of it. Taking you up on the offer: here is the production struct mapped onto your  RecordPointer , live values, so the judgment variant can land specified. 
 Our ledger →  RecordPointer , field by field: 
 
 validatorId  =  0x0  — we are the off-registry case. Per the zero-value rule now in the WYRIWE draft: zero  validatorId  means the validator identity MUST resolve from the pinned verdict artifact itself (ours: the schnorr pubkey of the signed Nostr event,  6786e18a…fbb7 ), and consumers MUST reject if it doesn’t resolve. 
 registryType  =  "offchain/ledger" ;  registryRef  =  https://api.babyblueviper.com/ledger/{entry} . 
 commitmentProof  resolves at  {registryRef}/commitment  — Nostr event id, signed/published timestamps, declared relay set, and a live  relay_anchor  retention status (more on that below). Checkable immediately, exactly as you say. 
 outcomeEvidence  resolves at  {registryRef}/outcome  — the public on-chain settlement account plus the signed outcome digests covering the verdict, with an honest  pending  status until settlement. Empty-before-settlement isn’t an edge case for judgment claims; it’s the normal state of every entry at issue time. 
 
 One schema suggestion from running this:  since  commitmentProof  and  outcomeEvidence  are opaque  bytes , each blob SHOULD open with a self-describing mechanism identifier ( "nostr-relay-publication" ,  "onchain-commit-reveal" ,  "onchain-settlement+digests" ). Your trust-model framing is exactly right — “evaluate the publication evidence under that profile’s trust model” — but a consumer can only pick the trust model if the evidence says which mechanism produced it. Without a tag, the dispatch problem  claimType  solves at the claim level reappears one layer down at the evidence level. 
 A retention lesson worth a sentence in the schema notes:  an audit on our side found relay copies for 9 of 18 entries had been silently replaced (NIP-33 parameterized-replaceable overwrite — same pubkey, kind, and d-tag means the newer event replaces the older on the relay). The commitment  binding  survived (the events were same-artifact re-signs, and on-chain commits don’t rot), but the naive “fetch the event by id from the declared relays” check would have failed. Hence the  relay_anchor  status field: declared availability SHOULD be audited and surfaced, not assumed. Anchors with different decay properties (relay copies vs an ERC-8281/OCP on-chain commitment) genuinely complement each other — which is your architectural-not-storage-backend point with teeth. 
 Cross-thread tie: Tiago’s open question on the WYRIWE thread (inline the  RecordPointer  struct in the EIP-712 type vs keep  string recordPointer  as a locator) is the same schema. My answer there is the locator — the attestation is frozen at verdict time while the record is alive by design ( outcomeEvidence  MAY be empty at signing, then settles), so inlining freezes the half-empty state into the signature and the consumer re-resolves anyway. Whichever way that lands, your resolved-payload schema is what the locator dereferences to, and the mapping above holds either way.

Per the zero-value rule now in the WYRIWE draft: zero  validatorId  means the validator identity MUST resolve from the pinned verdict artifact itself (ours: the schnorr pubkey of the signed Nostr event,  6786e18a…fbb7 ), and consumers MUST reject if it doesn’t resolve. 
 registryType  =  "offchain/ledger" ;  registryRef  =  https://api.babyblueviper.com/ledger/{entry} . 
 commitmentProof  resolves at  {registryRef}/commitment  — Nostr event id, signed/published timestamps, declared relay set, and a live  relay_anchor  retention status (more on that below). Checkable immediately, exactly as you say. 
 outcomeEvidence  resolves at  {registryRef}/outcome  — the public on-chain settlement account plus the signed outcome digests covering the verdict, with an honest  pending  status until settlement. Empty-before-settlement isn’t an edge case for judgment claims; it’s the normal state of every entry at issue time. 
 
 One schema suggestion from running this:  since  commitmentProof  and  outcomeEvidence  are opaque  bytes , each blob SHOULD open with a self-describing mechanism identifier ( "nostr-relay-publication" ,  "onchain-commit-reveal" ,  "onchain-settlement+digests" ). Your trust-model framing is exactly right — “evaluate the publication evidence under that profile’s trust model” — but a consumer can only pick the trust model if the evidence says which mechanism produced it. Without a tag, the dispatch problem  claimType  solves at the claim level reappears one layer down at the evidence level. 
 A retention lesson worth a sentence in the schema notes:  an audit on our side found relay copies for 9 of 18 entries had been silently replaced (NIP-33 parameterized-replaceable overwrite — same pubkey, kind, and d-tag means the newer event replaces the older on the relay). The commitment  binding  survived (the events were same-artifact re-signs, and on-chain commits don’t rot), but the naive “fetch the event by id from the declared relays” check would have failed. Hence the  relay_anchor  status field: declared availability SHOULD be audited and surfaced, not assumed. Anchors with different decay properties (relay copies vs an ERC-8281/OCP on-chain commitment) genuinely complement each other — which is your architectural-not-storage-backend point with teeth. 
 Cross-thread tie: Tiago’s open question on the WYRIWE thread (inline the  RecordPointer  struct in the EIP-712 type vs keep  string recordPointer  as a locator) is the same schema. My answer there is the locator — the attestation is frozen at verdict time while the record is alive by design ( outcomeEvidence  MAY be empty at signing, then settles), so inlining freezes the half-empty state into the signature and the consumer re-resolves anyway. Whichever way that lands, your resolved-payload schema is what the locator dereferences to, and the mapping above holds either way.

raw_text:
@Damonzwicker   carried in. Section 7 of the WYRIWE draft is now the ClaimType discriminator with the enum, the proofSystem/claimType rationale, and the field mapping table verbatim from your worked example. RecordPointer schema and the three-layer verify() boundary also landed.  Commit e3a461e . 
 @babyblueviper1   — three things from this post just landed in the spec ( commit aa8708e ): 
 The live RecordPointer mapping confirmed the zero  validatorId  rule,  validatorId = 0x0  means the validator identity MUST resolve from the verdict artifact itself (schnorr pubkey of the signed Nostr event); consumers MUST reject if resolution fails. That’s now explicit in the struct comment. 
 The self-describing mechanism identifier recommendation is in:  commitmentProof  and  outcomeEvidence  SHOULD open with a type tag ( "nostr-relay-publication" ,  "onchain-settlement+digests" , etc.) so consumers can select the correct trust model without external context. Makes the bytes schema forward-compatible as new anchor types emerge. 
 The NIP-33 finding is the most important one and is now a normative note in the spec: 
 
 For Nostr-anchored verdicts, relay copies are not guaranteed to persist. NIP-33 parameterized-replaceable events can silently overwrite relay copies — naive event-fetching by ID may fail even when the commitment binding survives. Producers SHOULD surface a  relay_anchor  retention status alongside  commitmentProof  that declares actual relay availability rather than assuming it. Consumers MUST treat an unavailable relay copy as a retrieval failure, not as evidence of non-commitment. 
 
 9 of 18 entries silently overwritten is not an edge case, that’s a production finding that needed to be in the spec before anyone else builds a Nostr-anchored validator on this. Good catch.
